game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1]Description[/h1]

Orwell is a visual novel that puts you in the shoes of a Big Brother employee: you are tasked with spying on people and uploading to the system anything suspicious. Unlike most visual novels, you are not presented here with walls of text followed by lists of choices. Rather, your interaction with the game and its unfolding story goes solely through the gimmick of uploading the data chunks you find (or not). By picking among conflicting data chunks or by choosing not to upload some sensitive information, you impact the story in small and big ways.

[h1]Pros[/h1]
[list]
[*] Fresh interaction gimmick that goes very well with the theme
[*] Credible writing with many characters each having their own style of speech
[*] Interesting choices going WAY beyond the good/bad dichotomy
[*] Decent art style
[*] Fair amount of consequences to choices made, though the game remains linear
[/list]

[h1]Cons[/h1]
[list]
[*] Notification system takes some getting used to ([spoiler]the system will sometimes find old information suddenly relevant, requiring you to regularly browse through the lists of documents to make sure no red star has popped[/spoiler])
[*] Because all chats and phone calls are delivered sloooooowly (and I found no way to speed them up), replaying the game to get the achievements or test other choices is a bit of a chore
[*] Political messages are (very) thinly veiled and might annoy (or even anger?) some players
[/list]

[h1]Verdict[/h1]

Do you hate it when someone tries to convey a political message artistically and ends up as subtle as a bull in a china shop? If so, stay away from this game. You're going to hate it.

Still here? OK, here's an idea: put yourself in the shoes of an orwellian enforcer and imagine the consequences of government trampling all over freedom, privacy and presumption of innocence.

Interested? Then try Orwell. Go in expecting a fresh visual novel and a politically charged (to the point of being heavy-handed at times) thought experiment. There is much to like.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] Game Summary: [/h1] 
This game doesn't fit into most normal game conventions and acts more like a cautionary tale.  By allowing the gamer to take the seat of a possible government agent in a program giving you so much power and access over people's lives, it lets you determine what you take away from it.  Is it a necessary evil for the government to have this much depth and access to what people are posting online, downloaded on their various devices, and talking about in their phone calls?  Or is that question alone already pushing too far, as people have an inherent right to privacy?  Wisely the game developer merely posits this to its audience, instead of preaching what is or isn't appropriate behavior in the 21st Century and beyond.  


[h1] Pros: [/h1] 
•	The first playthrough where I was intruding so far into people's lives made me feel uncomfortable.  Not scared or tense, just somewhat uncomfortable.  I think it's because invading people's privacy to this extent, knowing how easily the same thing could happen to you, is rather unsettling.  Medical records and mental health histories, various profiles and online communities you participate in (theoretically behind an alias), personal conversations and chats, all available for someone to read through.  For someone to comb through for any signs of instability, derangement, or evidence that this person isn't a law-abiding citizen, but a dirty crook.  This is dangerously close to criminalizing people for wrong-think.  
•	This game shines in its story and writing, because the characters feel real.  Their various profiles and conversations, how they become both paranoid and angry, but still only guessing at how bad things already are regarding the government's intrusion into their lives.  It gives the game a greater sense of reality and immersion, which is key.  They may not be rocket scientists, but they do take steps to avoid being screwed over, though if you're being a good big brother, it's already too late for them.  
•	I love that what I choose to upload can have a pretty big impact on how what the characters are saying and doing is interpreted.  It can either be seen as the acts of an innocent person, or the pattern of someone who's a low-down crook.  It raises the question of how any of us would look from the outside to someone who'd see all of our online activity.
•	The music acts as ambient background.  It's very low-key, and could theoretically be the sort of soft tune a government office would play to keep employees from getting too antsy.  This is for the most part, but when the climax of each day/act builds, then it picks up and gets you on edge.


[h1] Cons: [/h1] 
• 	Though it would take more time in both development and gameplay, it'd be nice if there were more people for you to look into who turned out to be red herrings.  It's not necessarily enjoyable being led astray, but it'd help sharpen the point of the game.  If you were being paranoid and looking at people through the lens of criminalizing everyone, you'd waste time and resources chasing false leads.  If you put on kids gloves and rationalized every viable threat as a misunderstanding, you'd let dangerous people slip on through.  What people say and mean aren't always the same, and one person's harmless rant is another's death threat.  
•	*Semi-Spoiler* I think one downside of the story is that all the key players are not inherently innocent.  They all have something significant to cover up, a reasonable way of implicating them for a crime and leading to their detention.  If they were merely guilty by association, and small phrases and statements were being pulled together to paint them as guilty, I think that would have had a stronger impact.  Otherwise, with how it is here, locking everybody up is justified.  You aren't throwing someone in jail who's wholly innocent.
•	Ironically, with how the last day plays out, you get so much material to look at, but are strictly limited on how much you can upload.  I get the idea of building tension this way, but I think it goes against what the game was going for.  The dilemma of the game wasn't in having to make a decision with so little information, but at digging for far too much, and falsely implicating innocent people on what you could piece together.  
•	Where the game suffers is through further playthroughs, as you see what happens if you try things a bit differently.  Since you're familiar with the characters, storyline, and reading their messages, it'd be nice if those could be sped up, instead of having to wait.  The chats are fairly crisp-paced considering they're supposed to be happening real-time, but it bogs down when you've seen it before.
•	Early in the game, video footage was used, and I thought that was going to come up again later.  I was quite disappointed that it only had a place in the game once, and I do feel misled that everything you analyze in the game is just text, whether a call, chat, or profile.
•	It'd be nice if some of the items which are definitively pointless and not useful anymore would be cleared away.  For instance, all the random news clips and headlines, since most of them had no pertinence to the exploration for more information.  
•	Sometimes I had a really hard time dragging points of interest into profiles or disabling them.  The controls were a bit floaty and annoying to work with.


[h1] Conclusion: [/h1] 
Whether we like it or not, whatever we post online is going to exist indefinitely.  Since so much information is out there, it does raise the issue of who would be keeping track of these matters, who might be lurking without our knowledge to try and keep tabs over us.  Whether it's the government or not, people can do some pretty sketchy things with computers, and this knowledge and power is a great temptation, tool, and force.  This game acts as a simulation for what can be done with that kind of power.  A bumbling buffoon who doesn't take it seriously, could allow guilty parties to slip out of facing justice.  An overly authoritarian and distrustful person could throw people behind bars for any minor infraction.  True, laws may have been broken, but should we throw away privacy and autonomy to catch such small fries?  We'd be foolish to hand over such power carelessly, as it could be so easily abused, but total restriction could also prevent heinous monsters from being caught and prosecuted.  These are hefty matters worthy of being discussed in the public sphere, and this game highlights both sides of that discussion.  If you're looking for a game in a conventional sense, you'd be disappointed, but if you're open to an experience with an important message at its core, Orwell has a lot to offer.  

Be careful if you write a reply or comment on this review.  You don't know who could be reading it.  It's alright if you don't necessarily agree with everything the government does, but don't be overly critical and certainly don't call for a revolution or anything CRAZY like that.  We'd HATE for there to be a group trying to overthrow the government, right?  Oh crap, I hear them at my door.  They're on to me!  Fight while you still can, don't be compliant, resist, fight on, fi-!  *Device has been disconnected*

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell: Keeping An Eye On You (in short, Orwell) is a five-part episodic narrative-driven mystery video game by Osmotic Studios set in a dystopian world in which the player assumes the role of a governmental operative who monitors surveillance sources to discovery national security threats. The game is named after the famed anti-totalitarian writer George Orwell and is inspired by themes established by his magnum opus novel, 1984.

The story in Orwell takes place in a country named The Nation which is governed by a contemporary authoritarian government known as The Party. Due to a series of events in the past, The Party passed the Safety Bill which expanded the government's capability to spy on its citizens in the name of national security. To accomplish this, the Ministry of Security, at the helm of Secretary of Security Catherine Delacroix, built a secret surveillance system codenamed Orwell. After a successful application and being selected from a pool of candidates, the player takes the role of an outsourced Orwell investigator who lives outside The Nation and is tasked, with the help of an assigned advisor going by the alias of Symes, to find evidence on the terrorist (individual or group) who caused a bomb explosion during a presumably peaceful protest in the populated Freedom Plaza in Bonton, the capital city of The Nation, destroying a statue and killing several people. The player soon stumbles upon an activist group called Thought who advocates for freedom of speech with anti-governmental sentiments, yet unaware of Orwell, who is entangled in the bombing incident. From there on, the player uses everything at their disposal to find evidence to expectantly incriminate their first suspect, Cassandra Watergate, an artist who was present at the Plaza shortly before the explosion.

The story occurs across five days (episodes) and what originally seemed like another day at the office, turns into an intricate roller-coaster of a journey full of conspiracy theories, deception and shocking revelations. The narrative in Orwell is exceptionally well-written and what keeps the player on their toes and constantly engaged. Just as things might get slightly monotonous now and again, the story always seems to throw you a new bone through unexpected plot twists and interestingly branched out paths shaped by your various choices and consequences. Even though the story occurs across a country, Orwell actually focuses on a small group of individuals despite the illusion it might give in the beginning, thus I did end up wishing more citizens were actually involved in the end. Whilst this is somewhat disappointing, it makes for a more focused story and does help to get better attached to those said characters, which Orwell succeeds in both aspects. Frankly, the overarching story and its thought-provoking themes, along with the interesting characters you encounter along your journey, albeit a touch stereotypical once in a while, are the selling points of Orwell, and I am delighted to report that it satisfied my itch for a robust adventure mystery game which I have not had for a while recently. Due to the nature of the game, I cannot talk more about the story nor discuss its outcomes at this point, as it is best to unravel and experience it yourself, but there are about four confirmed endings. The game’s length lies somewhere between 4 – 6 hours, which I personally completed in one sitting thanks to its captivating story which made me impatiently want to know what happens next, but I do wish it were longer.

All in all, Orwell's gameplay is akin to a visual novel, so there is not a lot of interactivity involved, but what it does, mechanically speaking, is very solid and straightforward. During investigations, the player has to do various tasks such as (1) browsing and reading through news articles, social media pages and databases, (2) hacking computers or mobile phones to access stored data, and (3) wiretapping conversations over the phone and messaging applications. Each one of these tasks displays various text passages in the form of datachuncks (highlighted by the game for the player’s ease) which could be uploaded on the surveillance system to piece together clues, construct evidence on suspects and, in theory, incriminate them. Each new datachunck uploaded updates a suspect’s profile with more information and occasionally even opens up profiles of new suspects in connection to the respective suspect as the plot thickens. You cannot undo an upload, so think carefully beforehand. Sometimes suspects give contradicting statements over the duration of the story through either dishonesty or unintended misinformation as the result of human nature, which you would then have to use your own judgement and decide which datachunck to upload to support the government’s case, or not. You see, the player can play by the rules to appease the government or ignore vital information to protect the suspects (depending on your moral compass), and either playstyle has several cleverly written consequences. The mechanics do feel too simplistic and repetitive but begin to shine in the second half of the game once there is a lot more information to chew and digest. Moreover, the adviser gives you bite-sized info as to what is happening during almost each one of your moves, so technically you should not feel lost with how the story unfolds. Plus, at the end of each day, a window summary displays all your findings and events that occurred on the day to be up to speed.

One major criticism I do have with its gameplay, however, is that despite the game warning the player that they are not required to upload every datachunk spotted, I always had the compulsion to upload everything I could find regardless since there is no penalty for doing so as far as I recall, aside for a handful of contradictions and, of course, the path of some key plot events. Retrospectively, I feel the game should have better incentivised the player to upload fewer datachuncks or increased contradictions to spice things up. Unfortunately, the game limits your number datachuncks uploads to create a nerve-wracking atmosphere (commendable mechanic) only at the end and I wish that was predominant throughout the entire game instead.

Visually, Orwell is all about the graphical user interface (of a computer monitor) since that is where you will be carrying out all your investigations and decision-making. The art style with its stylized polygonal pictures suits its dystopian themes and the presentation is sufficiently appealing thanks to its good use of appropriate colour pallets and well-designed page layouts. The interface is also intuitive and easy to navigate as a result of its slick design. Whilst the soundtrack is rather short and may seem minimal, it brilliantly captures the eerie atmosphere and even gets momentarily tenser when a plot twist occurs and stakes have risen. Considering there is plenty of reading and no voice acting involved, the tone and vibe of the soundtrack help it to never become distracting.

In conclusion, Orwell: Keeping An Eye On You is a fantastic, but short, mystery game set in a frightfully believable dystopian setting with a strong narrative that challenges your own ethics and presents balanced points of view in the long-lasting battle between the individual’s freedom and privacy versus the government’s security and surveillance. Whilst it is mechanically simplistic and not as diverse, nor challenging, as a game like Papers Please which shares a few familiar social commentaries, it is unique in its own right and worthy of a spiritual successor to 1984. At the end of the day, it is an interactive book more than a conventional adventure game where you might solve puzzles, which feels appropriate considering it is inspired by a novel. Definitely a must-play for George Orwell fans like myself and anyone interested in good mystery/detective games in the format of visual novels.

Stay vigilant.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Great game, I got it in the humble bundle monthly along with other games, and decided to play it because it looked interesting.

Describing the game, it's a very well made point and click adventure, but it's different from your typical point and click games because here you just use Orwell, an operating system designed to watch and monitor people, you can browse different websites and access all sorts of public and private information about your suspects, you go from page to page, phone to phone, computer to computer, device to device, as you try and look for useful information that may help you in your objectives.

The story is short but entertaining and exciting, you get the feeling of really becoming an Orwell 'investigator', the feeling is authentic, the websites, pages, profiles, articles, and that sort of stuff seemed believable enough to get you going into the story. Sometimes the story feels a little bit linear and forced upon you, e.g. pages that you need to look into for information will sometimes be spoonfed to you. but I get it though, if it wasn't though, many people won't know what to do next and get stuck, and they will need to add a lot more useless filler pages/information to make it a more realistic and harder experience. As typical with these kinds of games, there are multiple endings, all affected by your choices in the game. so it adds a bit of replay value.

review_text_raw:
I had a pretty good idea of what to expect when I started playing Orwell, but I was surprised time and time again about the absolutely amazing writing and the whole premise of the game. While not being overly complex in its mechanics, Orwell provides an emotional experience like few other games I have ever played and is able to capture the dystopian vibe of 1984 to an extremely disturbing level.

I started my first playthrough in the evening and it gripped me so much that I couldn't stop playing until I had finished the game some time around 3 a.m.

While the game doesn't offer a lot of choices, most of these actually do matter and then fold out in a logical way. Contrary to Telltale games, choices have an actual emotional impact on the player, which is something I haven't seen often in videogaming.

Everyone even remotely interested in storytelling and the workings of society should have played this to completion at least once. Especially people who think they have nothing to hide and don't see an issue with the paradigm of security above all. This game does actually successfully deliver a very disturbing perspective.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I've had bad experiences with plot-heavy games. Even Telltale's much celebrated titles did very little for me and have contributed to this theory I've had for a long time to video games, in general, seemed incapable of telling a good story. I've always believed that games were much stronger when focusing on mechanics, and those that sacrificed mechanics in favor of plot would always just create an inferior work compared to books or movies.

Orwell is an exception.

What at first might strike you as a fairly preachy "topic of the day" game managed to surpass all my expectations. From the beginning till the end, Orwell and it's characters captivated me.

Orwell is an elegant game. One that understands perfectly how to integrate the agency of it's players to fit into the narrative it's trying to weave, and does so well. Despite the fact that you simply play as a man behind a computer screen, your actions feel like they have consequences, even if sometimes those consequences are ones you don't intend. The longer I played the game, the more I thought about the consequences of every piece of information I submitted, pouring over every bit of data and agonizing over the tiniest nuances of dialogue

While Orwell's themes should be fairly evident from it's title and presentation, I found the plot to be intelligent and far from one-dimensional. Playing the game, often I thought to myself: "Did I make the right call?", "Should I really have told them about that?" I spent a good thirty minutes trying to decide on what I would do during the ending, and even as I write this review I question if I really did the right thing.

To me, that is the hallmark of a good story. One that engages you, makes you feel invested...and above all else; makes you care. It's been a while since I felt so compelled to write a recommendation. But Orwell is one of these games that comes once in a blue moon, and tend to get sadly overlooked. If you couldn't guess already, I highly recommend Orwell. It's one of the best experiences I've had with a story rich game to date, Osmotic Studios has done a fantastic job.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[b]Believable writing and gameplay mesh to bring the Orwellian nightmare to life.[/b]

[u][i]Summary:[/i][/u]
With [i]Orwell[/i] literally simulating a job, its success or failure as a game almost entirely hinges on the strength of its writing. Fortunately for all of us, it succeeds with flying colors. The characters it depicts are distinct and memorable. The scenarios it presents to you demand your full attention, else you miss something that leads to catastrophe. In the end it will leave you wondering how else things could have played out.

To be clear, [i]Orwell[/i] is an almost entirely text based experience. It mimics a work computer, including internet browser, email, and even a news and weather report. There is no voice acting, though the voice in my head for each of them is so strong that I had to pause and double check myself on that. Props again to the writers for that. The sound in the game sets a good atmosphere but is limited in quantity to the point of being noticeably repetitive.

If you can stomach the reading load, [i]Orwell[/i] is a novel game that is well worth your time and the cost of admission.

[u][i]Additional details:[/i][/u]
The visual style of [i]Orwell[/i] does an excellent job of being familiar enough to reality while also smoothing over reality's rough edges and mismatching designs. Throughout the game you'll uncover multiple pictures of the same character, often showing different sides of the person than you've seen before. For example you may first discover a finely manicured business photo before later discovering a photo of the same person out on the town, presumably a few drinks in and having a good time. Of course these aren't real photos, but artist renditions.

In order to discuss this next topic, I'll give you the most basic, spoiler free description of what you do in the game. You are tasked with investigating specific people and deciding whether what you find does or does not get added to a government database. Essentially you are both the spy and the filter between your target and the government. With that said, there were a few instances related to this that hampered my immersion. Generally it came from being required to enter a piece of information into the Big Brother system that I would have elected to keep private had it not been needed to progress.

I'll close with a few words on replayability. While there are multiple endings and outcomes to each chapter, I personally didn't feel compelled to replay more than a couple specific moments. The decisions that lead to each result are rarely obvious, so it's hard to go back and change things without reexamining things on a larger scale than I was interested in. There are guides out there that could speed up the process if you're so interested. I happily spent 9 hours with [i]Orwell[/i], nearly all of which was a single careful playthrough.

review_text_raw:
[quote][url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/7871885/]Follow our curator page:[b] OCG-Curations[/b] if you like and want to see more reviews like this one.[/url][/quote]

[h1]Overview:[/h1]
Orwell takes place in a distopian near future in the fictional city of Bonton in The Nation. Orwell is the codename of a vastly advanced surveilance system. They outsource investigations to outsiders of the nation - you! It is your task to spy on suspects and inform the government of what is going on. Basically, you roleplay as "Mr. FBI Man".

[h1]The Pros:[/h1]
[list]
[*][b]Interesting Story[/b] - The game is divided into five chapters, each representing a day in game. I won't be spoiling anything here so there isn't much to say, but I will state my overall impression. The story is good! If you take everything at face value you'll be in for a surprise when you realise this game is not as shallow as it may seem. Each chapter unveils another layer of mystery. There are also three endings (more on that later).

[*][b]Some Replayability[/b] - Every chapter has a few endings (usually two or three). After you finish the game, you may choose to replay starting from any chapter (subsequent ones are erased). Most unique paths you can take are linked to an achievement, so 100%-ing the game is pretty much just exploring every possibility. Don't get too exited though, as that took me about 8 hours and two playthroughs (but in the second one I did consult a guide to save time).

[*][b]Clean UI[/b] - I really like the clean, very intuitive interface. Which is good, considering as this UI is basically the whole game itself. The only downside is that it does not have a dark mode for playing at night, but it's not a dealbreaker.
[/list]

[h1]The Cons:[/h1]
[list]
[*][b]Hand Holding[/b] - You give information to Orwell by drag and dropping data chunks from your spy browser to the Orwell app. They are automatically outlined for you, which seems stupid, but it's a necesarry evil if you think about the programmers. However, one thing I don't like are the special chunks - the conflicts are highlighted in yellow, even if you didn't find both. This makes you extra careful before uploading as one makes the other invalid. This is how the story branches, but if you think about it it's a little stupid. How does the browser know about the conflict if you didn't access the other data chunk yet? This should be up to you - the "detective" to figure out. I wish they were all blue all the time, or turn yellow only after discovering both.

[*][b]Choices Almost Don't Matter[/b] - Remember when I said chapters? Well... they're pretty much isolated instances. Outcomes are mentioned from one to another, but only through slight dialogue changes. But the story progresses the same no matter what you do, until you reach chapter five and finally get to choose an ending.
[/list]

[h1]Conclusion:[/h1]
Orwell is a good game because it explores an interesting concept and offers a good story to boot. While it's not as mindbending as I first expected, I still recommended it as a very interactive visual novel. If the topic interests you and don't mind the short playtime, this is a good game to pick up.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell is only getting more relevant in the years since it’s release given it’s subject matter of government surveillance. It is kind of a visual novel puzzle game where you navigate different platforms finding bits of info that you can tag to the database which in turn can find you more info. As you go on you start to unravel a story of who was behind the bombings. The bits of info are highlighted so you can’t miss them and you also don’t always have to tag them. This is because some info is out of context. For instance someone saying that they are being tortured by cupcakes is obviously not actual torture but you can still tag the person involved as a torturer. Having the discretion is nice but there are other times where you have to tag certain data to progress that I don’t feel was data that must have been tagged or as relevant as the game made it. I also don’t like how you can’t untag data. I also felt that at the end of the game there was supposed to be multiple ways to handle the outcome but I could only see one or possibly two. I don’t know why the other ways weren’t available to me as I can’t think of a story reason that I shouldn’t have been able to pull off what i wanted. The story was good but the twists near the end were simply fantastic. The UI for the game was easy to get used to and had a good design. I also liked how new parts of the software were revealed as they became needed. The game has no voice acting but that wasn’t an issue wand made sense given the fact that outside of recorded calls this was all  just you at a computer. The puzzle aspect was that you have to scour the various blogs; calls; emails; etc to find info you can use to further the game as well as provide additional depth details and context. 

	I played Orwell on Linux. It froze on me once but other than that I encountered no issues and noticed no spelling errors. There are no graphics options and the game has a 60 FPS cap. You can save on exit but there is just one save slot so you can’t undo choices or have multiple save files. Performance was good with no noticeable lag. Alt-Tab Didn’t work.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I wrote this review after 3 episodes, I might change it later.

Orwell is an interesting game about collecting personal data from people through various means (social media, dating sites, phone calls etc.) and investigating to find the terrorist/s that plant bombs in public places. The gameplay reminds me a lot of Analogue : Hate Story, which is a good sign. Every document gives you new informations, that leads you to new documents etc.

Overall the writing is very solid and believable, you can only see typed messages but they all express the character's personality : the lawyer is writing slowly with perfect punctuation, the young activist uses slang and typos etc. Sometimes there are some blatant shortcuts designed for exposition (a conversation with an unknown person that starts with "What can I do for you, Susan Mills, my best friend from Hugand University ?") but it didn't bother me too much.

What bothers me however is how much the game holds your hand. You can only select a few informations and only about the suspect "du jour". Several times I thought "Wow, Alan is very suspect !" but I couldn't get any informations about him until the next day where I'm told "Today we'll focus on Alan, he's suspect". Am I the investigator or just a goddamn clerk ?

It led to a very aggravating moment where I had to chose between two options, I took the wrong one and innocent people died. To add insult to injury, my sidekick had the nerve to patronize me "What did we do wrong ? If we had taken the other option, this could have been avoided". I think it was meant to emotionally disturb me and make me think that this investigation method is fundamentally flawed, on top of being ethically reprehensible. But instead all I could think was "F*ck you, all informations you ALLOWED me to get pointed at the first option being the good one. You think you're cleverly ambiguous but you're just a cheap mystery novel deliberately misleading the audience to make the plot last long enough".

In conclusion, an extremely lukewarm approval, that might lead to a disapproval if they keep doing this in future episodes. I don't want to replay this game as it feels like Telltale's Walking Dead, where the illusion of choice disappears at the second playthrough where different choices don't impact as much as they seemed.

EDIT : I finished the 5 chapters, I keep my extremely uncommitted approval (lets say 50.1/100).
What limits this game the most is its linearity. I compared it to a mystery novel, it's even worse in late episodes, they want you to suspect specific people in specific orders punctuated by specific twists. You learn in chapter 5 crucial informations that you had no reason not to discover in chapters 1 and 2, since you follow the exact same protocol except the game deliberately kept informations away from you in order to make the game last 5 chapters.

The game also has the nerve to make this railroad look like a social commentary. "You've been chasing the wrong people the entire time, this is the proof that Orwell is unreliable !". Yeah but no, this is just proof that you're putting arbitrary limitations for the sake of the narrative. And even with that, Orwell did better than any other investigation method. Call it unethical, dangerous, tyrannical if you want, but it gets sh*t done and saved lives, and would have done even better without the railroad.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
A surprisingly immersive psuedo-visual novel that plays on the tropes of governmental surveillance in a way that makes you question every action that you make in the game. The writing is absolutely try-hard sometimes, to the point of being cringey only on rare occasions, but the overall story is interesting and captivating in a way that kept me on the edge of my seat the whole way through. You really begin to feel that you are an investigator, prying into the personal life of these people, and for a game so simple to do that is absolutely fantastic imo.

The mechanics are simple point, click, drag. The gameplay itself requires deducing events and character motivation through the combination of various news sources, emails, and hacked text messages. It requires a lot of reading and more thinking than I anticipated, leaving me stumped a few more times than I care to admit, but it doesn't feel boring in the slightest.

It's short, it's sweet, and it's to the point. I would recommend it to anyone that likes narrative experiences.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1]What Orwell is[/h1]

This is likely the first thing you might ask yourself if you're considering buying this game. Basically Orwell is a visual novel. The main way the game communicates is through text and the way you progress the story is by character dialogue. The way you trigger the dialogue is the unusual part. Basically you're a government employee whose job is to spy on people and while you do it by reading their e-mails, browsing their facebook page you're highlighted info you might want to add to the government's archive and investigate it. 

[h1]The Good[/h1]

The way the characters unfold is pulled off incredibly well. Despite me being quite the cynical person the game affected me too when I learned about the people's secrets and their motivations behind their actions. I'm being purposefully vague as I don't want to spoil anything. The art style is also quite unique, albeit it's explained poorly (viewing the world through chunks of data and all that). Another plus is that the game is all text so you could run it on anything. I'm sure an android port would be a piece of cake, and you could also play it on your grandma's chromebook.

[h1]The not-so-good[/h1]

The budget constraints were clear as day to me. The phone calls were all text so they weren't any different from the chat conversations, which broke immersion to me. Some voice acting would have elevated things a lot. Another minus is the way the narrative is presented at times. The character archetypes (hacker, government official, shy girl, punk kid) were really stereotypical and made the otherwise heavy dystopian story feel juvenile and borderline teen comedy-esque. The political commentary seemed really black and white, "good guys vs. bad guys" type of story. All the government officials act incredibly arrogant, almost like cartoon villains and all the civilian characters, as stated above, are just plain archetypes (with a few exceptions). So the game could have done a little better in the writing department.

[h1]The Verdict[/h1]

Orwell is a great visual novel game with a twist, that suffers from a lack of scale (likely due to a limited budget) and some writing flaws, but is overall superb for what it is. Definitely recommended, just don't expect the best game you've ever played.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Goodness, when was the last time I one-shotted a game? Just finished Orwell, having only taken a break for supper, and boy what a game. Bravo to everyone involved.

I think the game first of all deserves plaudits for style and storytelling, interwoven into gameplay. This kind of indie game really shows what's capable in interactive media, including making the player a participant in the activities. No two ways about it, you don't walk away with clean hands from this narritive. And god, that's just unbelievably cool. I can't think of any other medium that works as well. By uncovering the stories that these characters contain, the player gets pulled into the drama and hell, I'd say I believe these characters more than I would in a traditional triple-A game narritive. This is partially due to the strength of the writing but also due to the computer interface framing device which allows for a completely seamless experience.

But what this game really does well is play with its themes. It's a power trip, to dig through people's lives and find the bits and pieces that fit into a story that you can tell someone else. It's also remarkably disturbing how plausible it all is, and how effectively the player can go about their business. As I played, I started wondering to myself how much art might imitate life. How far away are we from the very horror portrayed here? How do we defeat such a tool? Is there anywhere else to go after that?

The game also does a great job of leaving a very plausible trail of breadcrumbs to follow, with a good amount of leeway into what needs to be found and in what order. The actual layout of the story isn't entirely known to me (what exactly is cleverly scripted) but I'd say the rails are actually fairly wide at parts, and usually coming to a head with each chapter. The space to move around here is necessary both to keep the player engaged and addicted, but also to make the simulation seem plausible. If the story was too narrow it would feel a bit too pre-arranged, but there's some actual detective work to do here and that's quite marvelous, if not novel.

For those on the fence, play this game. Completely worth your 5 hours. With a chaser of Citizenfour while you're at it. Crazy that I'm playing with the notion of a game properly adding to the political discourse, yet here we are. I suspect this game will linger with me for a long while.

Don't mind my playtime, I've played and finished this game on another platform so it's not counted here.
I can absolutely say that this game is very brilliant. From the UI design which makes you feel like you're really working from home on your own computer, to the story, which is very well written and developed.

The more you go on with the story, if you really pay attention to the details, the more the plot twist becames obvious, but it's certainly nothing you might expect from the beginning.

It's kinda short, and if you're not a fan of the genre it might be a little boring, since the things you do, except for those you can decide on, are actually driven and highlited by the game itself, so the interaction is almost limited to what the game wants you to do, but again, if you like the genre, the main feature of this game is actually the story, and the fact that you can discover it only bit by bit, by reading all the information given.

Currently this game is on sale, together with the second one in a bundle, and for less more than 4€ is totally a must-buy.

Small digression on the translation: I played the game with the Italian translation because that's my main language, the game started automatically in that language and it seemed ok in the beginning.
Sadly, the more it goes on, the more it gets worse. Some translated sentences are even totally senseless and sometimes it gets a little frustrating to read, since the game is based on reading info.
I understand that even if it's very bad it might be useful for people who can't read English, but I only wish I had a way to switch to English language in-game, so that I could have changed language while playing.

[i]Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You[/i] is a tense, thought-provoking surveillance thriller that does more with a few browser tabs and text files than most games do with entire cities. It casts you as a government contractor sifting through personal data to uncover a growing threat—and forces you to wrestle with how much “truth” you really need to keep people safe. It’s slick, unsettling, and surprisingly emotional.

[b]🪬 Pros:[/b]
[list]
[*] Brilliant UI that doubles as storytelling. The whole game takes place inside a simulated desktop, with tabs for social media, chat logs, police records, and more. But it’s not just aesthetic! It feels like doing a job. Every click, every search result, every drag-and-drop data point creates tension. The interface is intuitive, immersive, and sinister.

[*] Deep moral ambiguity in every decision. Do you report that someone once expressed violent thoughts in a song lyric? Do you include their real name in a classified file? What about the context? The game forces you to make hard calls on limited info, and the consequences are immediate. 

[*] Tightly written and emotionally resonant. Despite being mostly text, the characters come alive through their messages, posts, and private calls. You start to see their contradictions, their fears, their humor. It’s intimate in a way that hits hard when you're the one deciding what gets flagged—and what gets buried.

[*] Great balance of investigation and puzzle-solving. The game isn’t about cracking codes or hacking firewalls: it’s about connecting dots. Who knows who? What’s fact, what’s hearsay, and what might get someone arrested? You feel clever when you catch a subtle connection between a dating profile and a news article. It’s simple but deeply satisfying.

[*] Fantastic pacing and structure. The game unfolds over five episodes, each building tension and complexity. Just when you think you know what’s going on, it flips your assumptions. It’s rare to find a game this compact that still manages to feel complete and impactful.
[/list]

👁️ [b]Cons:[/b]
[list]
[*] Limited replay value. While your choices do have consequences, the story arc mostly funnels toward the same endpoint with slight variations. It’s a brilliant one-time experience, but it may not have the branching depth to support multiple playthroughs.

[*] Some plot twists feel a bit on-the-nose. The writing is mostly subtle, but a few characters and twists lean heavily into dystopian clichés. It's forgivable, especially for a debut game, but occasionally the nuance slips.

[*] A bit short. For players used to longer visual novels or narrative-driven games, [i]Orwell[/i] might feel more like an extended episode than a full series. That said, it’s tightly packed and doesn’t waste your time.
[/list]

review_text_raw:
[i] *very, very minor spoilers are hidden* [/i]

[h1] TL;DR "The Last Enemy" without Cucumberpatch [/h1]

Admittedly, the above reference might skate over a few people's heads, but the core themes are the same. Based loosely around the old US Total Information Awareness system, the game explores the issues around predictive profiling and human bias.

The details are what makes this game shine: The irrelevant online junk, the typos and slang, the shoddy dating websites, even the pages load like a real browser. The user interface is slick and easy to use. For that extra immersion, I really recommend taking your time to read as much as you can. It's not as quirky as DX:HR, but it's close.

The characters are wonderfully complex, if occasionally stereotypical. I love the "show, don't tell" approach of implying their personalities through online interactions, and the format of the game is really unique -- I've never played a game quite like this before.

My biggest gripe is gameplay. There is none. Everything is highlighted and every conflict displayed, which underwhelms the idea that [spoiler] your bias invalidates Orwell [/spoiler], and eventually turns the game into a mindless point-and-click. There are no difficult puzzles or decisions beyond moral ones, and even those seem to have little bearing on the outcome. The ending certainly felt a little shoehorned, and the [spoiler] twist a little out of character [/spoiler]. It's best to view this game as an interactive story rather than a game. I'd have also liked the ability to replay individual episodes - restarting the game just to change a single decision in ep. 5 is a little inconvenient.

As a very fast reader, the entire game took 3-4 hours to complete, bearing in mind I read absolutely everything. Half the time seems to be spent on watching conversations scroll in real time, which is realistic, but not for the impatient. If you don't like reading or text-based games, don't bother.

I really do recommend this game. The tense, compelling plot had me eagerly waiting for the next episode. You do become emotionally involved with the characters, even with a week between episodes. A little shallow at times, but enjoyable nonetheless.

11/10 would hack the local fishing society again.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
The premise is simple:
It's a game where you play a investigator who works for the government, sifting through data in all of its forms in order to fight for the safety of the public in the fictional world that it's set in.

There have been many 'hacking' games that have come out over the years, but Orwell takes the idea and puts you in the position of 'good' rather than 'bad', which creates the core ideology of the game -- If what you're doing is so good, then why do you feel so bad doing it?

The game proceeds along a UI of sorts, one that allows you to sift through websites, personal pages and even listen on some incredibly well-simulated 'real time chats', along with interruptions and intentional spelling errors that betray the typer's emotions and mental states. It's one of the best simulations of texting I've seen before in a game, and it DOES stand out. The articles and websites, while simple and clean, are detailed and packed full of worldbuilding -- the developers go out of their way to fill the world with detail that was never necessary to get from point A to B, but still fill everything with life and activity, and the world ends up feeling a little bit less compartmentalized than other games which force you into a limited POV.

However, this all leads back to the internal condundrum I have with this game:
You work with a handler who analyses the information you send him, and it's his job to make sense of it all. All you do is forward him the pertinent information, enough for him to make decisions and calls on how to handle situations. And you must choose what it is you want to send.

It's your choice to pick A over B. And it's not outright lies, because you're the good guy, remember? But whatever you send can tinge a thought, affect outcomes and colour perceptions in slight, yet pertinent, ways. Your own analysis plays a big part in how you want to portray someone else, and ultimately, the only one who has to live with the decisions you make is yourself.

Orwell is a great game about people, but more than that, it's a platform to help you examine yourself as a person. Since you're doing this for the percieved good, what decisions will you make and how far will you go to get what you want? And is there ever a time when personal freedom can be infringed upon for the greater result? Well... that might be another question for another time.

It's a good game tho, eh?

(( P.S.: Like any other 'visual novel' style game, and including the horrendous works of Mr. David Cage, I am fully aware that some of these 'choices' may be nothing more than illusionary. However, the game does it well enough in its context that reflecting upon the choices you make actually makes more than just a surface-level difference since you're playing not a character, but yourself. And considering the game's name and influences, I believe this to be the point. ))

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[b]TL:DR: [/b] Does 1984 ring a bell? Yes? You are all good, skip this. No? Block off four hours and prepare a lighthearted movie after to flush the existential horror.

[h1]What is Orwell?[/h1]
The player takes the role of an independent third party taking the reigns of the most powerful surveillance technology ever built tasked with the investigation of a terrorist attack on a monument in the capital of a fictitious country called The Nation. Armed with a context sensitive browser the player dives head first into one medium deep rabbit hole.

[h1]Game Design | The Awesome (+2)[/h1]
I adore the brutalist functionality of the game design. It feels like a desk job. There is nothing special to it. Everything works as one would expect it to. It should feel cold. It should provide a degree of separation from the subject while not hindering gameplay. This is one of the hardest tricks any game designer can pull off. Take it from a boring person who unironically loves to create spreadsheets for any number of things. This [i]rocks[/i].

[h1]Audio design | The Terrible (-2)[/h1]
Coming in on the opposite side of the spectrum is audio design. Or lack thereof. The only notable attempt at anything are dynamic music changes when the player comes across [i]shocking[/i] new information. And yes, I am exaggerating, because the music is exaggerating. The whiplash from the norm is that great. It arrives suddenly and leaves before it had a chance to order a frickin' latte. Then there are all the missed opportunities. The player has access to various types of data from texts, to web pages, to voice calls. Instead of a transcript it would have been great to have the few calls fully voiced. It would have brought the player even closer to the characters.

[h1]Characters | The Bad (-1)[/h1]
...of which Orwell utilizes several one dimensional archetypes with a couple of exceptions that show a hint of a second dimension. Fortunately for the game, the player is not forced to linger on any of the cast. We get just as much as we need to understand from where the wind is blowing before moving on to the next person. For better or worse, commentary on surveillance killing the human experience acts as the main character of the game and is largely responsible for the ankle deep depth of the human pawns.

[h1]Closing Thoughts | The Adequate (0)[/h1]
Orwell is a tricky proposition. On one side it is concise, excellently showcases pitfalls of absolute surveillance and should be a mandatory play on any high school, on the other side it is cynical to the core and does not allow a solution of the privacy/security conundrum. I could speculate that the original intention of the authors was to show the only winning move is not to play. However, I am writing this script seven years after the release in a world that is inching closer and closer to a world of AI driven absolute surveillance. The absolute surveillance of Orwell fails even with a human at the helm of its moral compass, what chance do we have in the real world without such an agent? At the end of the day art is a reflection of our perceived reality. I understand that having no way out nets a more chilling experience. However, if the resolution does not provide a positive outlook, something to aspire to, it leaves the observer in a very dark place.

[hr][/hr]

[h4]Note[/h4]
Individual sections (and the whole game) are critiqued on a scale of [i]The Terrible (-2)[/i] from the worse to [i]The Awesome (+2)[/i].

Great. Decided to check it absolutely randomly, when my main PC was in repair and I was looking for something simple for my working laptop. Honestly, never thought that it is possible to create an interesting story and gameplay... just from reading messages, chat and newspaper articles. In fact, this concept is indeed viable and works really good. It was very exciting to collect all these tiny pieces of information and investigate local story. Your actions have consequences and you decide how the story goes and how will it end. And yeah, it has some replay value.

What I especially would like to mention - great work with localization. Usually most developers deliver something formal and just for a checkmark (or no localization at all). Thus, in most cases I don't even bother to check it and just play in English. However, the game offered me to play in my language right away, so I decided to give it a chance. And the quality in indeed great. If indie studio is capable to do it, it's even more pathetic when big and greedy studios and their shills often find numerous excuses not to translate their games into more languages.

review_text_raw:
The idea is excellent: You're an operative tasked with monitoring the social media and activities of various individuals suspected of or likely to carry out terrorist attacks, with the goal of stopping them. Initially, everything seems quite obvious and trivial, but it soon begins to explore gray areas and presents very interesting moral dilemmas.

After playing through it a couple of times, you become aware of the intricate plot and how linear it is, but during your first playthrough, it's practically imperceptible. It manages to create a strong sense of decision-making and truly draw you into its narrative. You genuinely feel like a spy because perhaps that's exactly what your job would look like if you were one. You would stop seeing people as individuals and begin to see them as pixels. That's the magic of Orwell.

The only important point to note is that it's heavily dependent on the language you speak. If the game isn't in a language you're fluent in, I recommend not playing it, as the game demands a lot from you in interpreting very specific data and dialogue, which could cause you to miss some excellent details that enhance the experience.

This is a very interesting game, especially for anyone who has an interest in the surveillance state and the pros and cons of such a thing, mixed in with choices that really seem to matter.  I will admit that I have have, at the time of writing this review only played one playthrough, but the story was compelling and the information that I chose to put in/leave out really seemed to impact what was happening.  On top of that, the story is compelling, interesting and told through a very interesting way, feeding you snippets as you dig through the personal lives and media presence of several NPCs with various connections to one another, with a simple lock-off system that makes sense in-universe (we don't have clearance to investigate this person who has some connection to a potential suspect).

Beyond that, the only real issue I have with the game is the few interface bugs. game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
The focus here is fantastic writing.
The developers have crafted an atmosphere, which forces you to be part of the story.
Not as as the main character, but as an arbitrator who facilitates the continued flow of the story.
But as you follow the story, finding out each new snippet of information, seeing how the tangled web of interconnectedness grows, you are drawn in. Deeper and deeper into the story.

I'm hooked. I'm completely fascinated by the story.
As of this review, I just finished Episode 3. And I am feeling... a mixture of feelings.
Excitement as to what will happen next, but also sadness. 
And a deep feeling of personal responsibility how my actions or inaction may have led to each part of the story as it unfolds.

And that is a testament of the fantastic writing from the team behind this game. A dedication to their craft, and clever worldbuilding. 

It's been a long time since a game has affected me so deeply like this. 

This story will keep you in suspense, as there is no way to predict what will happen next. And I love it.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[b]”An interactive dystopian detective novel at its best”[/b]
 
[h1]The Good[/h1]
 
Orwell is an electrifying, Orwellian, (surprisingly enough) thriller with exciting twists and turns everywhere you look. The varied choices and the believable medium through which they are presented breathe so much life into the world and its characters. The mechanics, while there aren’t many to play with and master, they are polished and intuitive enough to get the point across in a believable manner. The writing and world building have to carry the game almost entirely and I can gladly say Osmotic Studios has delivered in this regard! Further to add to this, the pacing fits well into a fairly short experience, around 4 hours, which allows for easy and frequent replayability.
The choices you make are integral to the twists and turns you take. The way the choices are handled in Orwell are often left ambiguous with their outcome and effect on the world around you. Even then, every choice you make feels as though it has an impact on the world, no matter how small.
 
[h1]The Bad[/h1]
 
Certain aspects of the game can fell sluggish, such as the tiresome phone call logs and the constant (seemingly) dead ends on web pages. There can be a case made for these moments, however, since they do add to the overall integrity of this fictional world. My only fear is that some players may feel a bit disappointed during these moments that are paced so much slower than the bits in which the player is in direct control.
Another personal gripe with this game is that it’s cast, and plot can feel too expansive given the short time period the game takes place over. Certain events can completely go over the player’s head what with so many people and connections to remember.
 
[h1]The Verdict[/h1]
 
Orwell is an excellent example of compelling and effective storytelling told through the interactive medium of video games. It’s easy to get into and while it may not be the easiest narrative to understand, the writing will keep you engaged constantly. However, at times the story does slow down, and it is easy to get fatigued with the sheer amount of writing in this game.
I think it’s easiest to sum up Orwell as an interactive, dystopian, detective novel at its best. In a game that hinges on the “choices matter” idea, it does well in treating the player like an intelligent and competent participant. You have the ability to make inferences that might not accomplish what you’re trying to do. Also, it is important to note that in a game whose themes are centered around a battling of ideals the player’s choices are remarked upon by all characters and it is easy to let your biases make choices for you. I really do recommend this game to those of you that are itching to fit into the shoes of a detective that is a 3rd party in a war of ideals. Be careful with those choices of yours though, you never know who’s watching.
 
[h1]8/10[/h1]

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell stars you, the player, as an investigator in the Nation's (a stand-in for an unholy almagamation of the United States and the United Kingdom) new, government-ordained spying programme. Your job is to investigate suspected terrorists and cherrypick data you've acquired via researching the Internet and spying directly on their conversations, phones, and computers. You upload these data modules to the Orwell database and help construct a profile of these suspects that your advisor (who can't see your research sources in an effort to maintain some sort of ethical loophole) then uses to report back to the authorities, thus causing your actions to have potentially devastating consequences.

I've seen a few people complain about the gameplay--you are, essentially, dragging these data modules from one part of your screen to another (and, frustratingly, it can take a few clicks to get hold of them), which sounds unexciting on paper. But the story is compelling, and it's through this (slightly repetitive and boring) gameplay that you unlock the story, which can branch depending on which data you upload to Orwell. Some of it you have to, some of it you don't--and some of it you can use to alter the perception of certain suspects by picking which element of contradicting data you want to show to the advisor. 

The game does a very good job of highlighting how people become complacent with this level of privacy invasion--I've seen complaints of the game handholding you throughout, but, in my opinion, this helps you to slip into the mindset of uploading whatever data you come across, mindlessly painting suspects as victims because it's what your advisor wants of you. It wasn't until the end of my first playthrough that I realised how much damage I'd caused by providing evidence to suggest that innocent people were guilty of crimes they hadn't committed, and how many of the characters I'd either had arrested or killed via my actions of "innocuously" collecting their data. Which I guess is what the game wants you to do, particularly on a first playthrough.

That's not to say I don't have complaints. The game wants you to play multiple playthroughs, even if only to collect all of the achievements (most of which can be acquired in two playthroughs; two require a third, or replaying chapters on one of your profiles). Different actions have different outcomes and dialogue, and that produces slightly new scenes to watch (or, really, read). The problem is that the texts and calls you have to monitor can be so tediously long, particularly with little deviation--the last chapter has one that's just about shy of 10 minutes, and you can't do anything but sit and let it play. There's no option to skip the scene. 

I've also seen a few people complain that the game thinks people can never lie or exaggerate, which I assume refers to options where you can report suspects for having outspoken anti-government tendencies... but again, I think this is overlooking what the game wants you to consider. 

I highly recommend Orwell, although I bought it in the Humble Bundle and so bought it for much cheaper than its standard price--and I've already collected all the achievements in just over 6 hours of play, which isn't quite a £1 = 1 hour of playtime at its normal price. It's obviously not a game that's appealing to everyone, but I do think for those that like immersive visual novels with political themes (and that's essentially what it is), you'll enjoy Orwell.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Play as an investigator in a new secret gov. program named 'Orwell' that -- unsurprisingly -- spies on its own citizens' e-mails, phone conversations, laptops, etc., and selectively hunts for evidence of unlawful activity. The focus in this 5-part story is anti-governmental terrorism.

The name Orwell is on the nose, of course, and the writing is mostly along those lines. (This game is all text, all writing, so this is very important!) It, however, begins unraveling near the end, reaching for genuine philosophical depth. A favorite moment that's a bit too prescient is at the end while digging through the (optional) files that led to Orwell's creation. One of the creators calls the program Orwellian in its sinister direction. It's meant as a pejorative. The other creators have no idea who Orwell is -- one of the most famous English writers of the 20th century, and most influential on pop culture for over 50 years. They just think Orwell is a cool name, and so they use it unironically to name their entire Orwellian program. 

Do you see what's neat here?

I went in thinking Orwell didn't exist in this game's universe. But he does. And he's still a huge influence. The fictional government is so ignorant, run by idiots hell-bent on imaginary terrorism and protecting themselves and their interests, though, that the messages of Orwell's books are lost on them -- and they just don't care. 

This should sound familiar. This game felt like a fluffy beach-read dystopia in 2016, but it quickly turned accurate once January 20th rolled around in 2017. Awesome.

review_text_raw:
Wow I am more than impressed with this game. I am a big fan of the game genre of "Papers, Please", "This is the police" and similar games. I think when games explore your morals and hits you right in your cognitive dissonance. This game does this incredibly well. Surveilence is a difficult subject. There are pros and cons that vary between people.

This game sets your objective as having you aid in finding the suspect for a terrorist attack. This is of course a justifiable action and is in good favor for the public. You quickly start having conflicting thoughts about whether the people you're spying on and the information you gather is relevant at all. I am the type of person who is really interested in other people's affairs. This game absolutely worked wonders on this quirk of mine because I found it difficult to resist to look deeper in people's personal lives. I bet you will too constantly convince yourself that "this guy's past relationship drama might prove useful later".

The writing in this game is absolutely amazing in my honest opinion. This game felt real. The information layout, news articles, blogs, emails, texts, calls all felt real. The way you quickly progress from getting basic information on one person such as their name and occupation suddenly turns into having direct sneaky access to their desktop files, bank account activity and search history. You will find a lot of surprises in this game and lots of VERY difficult choices. There is a lot of conflicting ideas this game forces on you. For example you are presented with 2 or 3 very contradicting pieces of information. Sometimes it is easy to choose based on the source of where this info came from but when the consequences are severe, you are under pressure to make the right choice as there is no going back.

One downfall of this game is that there are some slight errors in the scripting that messes up the flow. For example there are certain bits which I suppose are meant to be discovered in a certain sequence but its possible to do it in the wrong sequence, resulting in dialogue that doesn't fit in. Alerting the higher ups of a threat after it already happened results in them thanking you for the useful information and that they will be prepared...even though this happened just recently and they were not prepared. The game also decides on itself which information is relevant or not and kind of makes you feel bad for collecting everything you might feel is necessary but thankfully you are not outright punished for it. Another big error I noticed was with relationships. I find out that a character has been married in the past and add it to the database but the database instead labels the character as currently married which is considered as wrong information until you find out more details later.

All in all these negatives do not affect the game much. This game is worth full price and I think is a must buy with a discount.
